M&A activity among asset management firms is skyrocketing:

Global asset management deal volumes are up to $53.8 billion year-to-date, the highest level on record in data going back to 1995.

This measures the combined value of announced mergers and acquisitions between fund management firms.

This is already ~$26.0 billion above the full-year 2025 amount and has surpassed the previous full-year record of ~$47 billion in 2024.

This comes as fund firms race for scale and broader reach across geographies and asset classes amid intensifying industry-wide competition.

Fee pressure and competition from low-cost index funds are squeezing smaller managers, making scale increasingly critical to remain competitive.

The asset management industry is consolidating at a historic pace.

US consumers are planning to cut back on spending:

The proportion of consumers planning to spend more on restaurants, bars, and take out over the next 6 months fell -2 percentage points in August, to ~24.5%, the 2nd-lowest since September 2025.

US consumers expecting to spend more on health care services fell -3 percentage points in August, to ~19.5%, the lowest since September 2025.

This also marks the steepest monthly decline among the top 5 categories tracked by the Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Survey.

At the same time, just ~21.5% of consumers now expect to spend more on beauty and personal care, down -1 percentage point from July and the lowest level since November 2025.

Furthermore, ~22.0% of consumers expect to spend more on streaming, internet, and mobile services, down -1 percentage point from the prior month, the 2nd-lowest since November 2025.

Consumers are pulling back on spending plans.

The US housing market is exceptionally weak:

The US Pending Home Sales Index fell -2.3% MoM in July, to 71.2 points, the 2nd-lowest on record.

The gauge has collapsed -36% since July 2021 and remains down -33% from pre-pandemic levels.

Last month’s weakness was broad-based, with all 4 major US regions posting monthly declines.

The West recorded the steepest drop, falling -7.7% MoM to an all-time low, now -47.4% below its July 2021 level.

The South, the nation's largest home-selling region, fell -2.2% MoM to its lowest level since January 2025, down -36.2% since July 2021.

At the same time, pending home sales in the Northeast decreased -2.0% MoM, down -31.2% over the last 5 years.

US housing activity continues to deteriorate.

The world's major central banks have finally unwound most of their pandemic-era balance sheet growth:

The Federal Reserve’s total assets as a % of US GDP are down to 21%, the lowest percentage since the 2020 pandemic.

By comparison, the peak was recorded in 2021 at ~37%.

At the same time, European Central Bank assets as a % of Eurozone GDP fell below 40% for the first time since Q1 2020, from the ~65% peak in 2022.

Total assets on the Bank of Japan’s balance sheet as a % of Japanese GDP are down to ~103%, their lowest since 2020, from the ~130% high in 2021.

The Bank of England’s assets are down to ~21% of UK GDP, the lowest since 2016, from the ~40% peak in 2021.

The pandemic-era central bank stimulus is largely gone.
Great news 🗞️!

Energy stocks have rarely seen this much hedge fund demand:

Hedge funds bought the most global energy stocks in almost 4 years last week.

This also marks their 12th weekly purchase over the last 13 weeks.

As a result, hedge funds are now the most overweight energy relative to global stocks since June 2024.

This marks a sharp reversal from their most underweight positioning since 2021, recorded in February 2026.

The only period where hedge funds had a materially larger energy exposure relative to global equities was during the 2022 energy bull market.

The energy trade is becoming increasingly crowded.

It’s telling that the Treasury’s actions last week to buy back more long-dated paper and issue more Bills took down the dollar and caused both gold and Bitcoin to soar. The market senses a slippery slope towards fiscal dominance and a possible loss in Fed independence. The assumption here is that for the Treasury to be successful in keeping yields down, it will need to significantly increase the size of the buybacks. That might require the Fed to become complicit in this operation twist, which takes us down the debasement path.  Loose fiscal policy combined with loose monetary policy is a clear negative for the dollar (which is sitting on a long term trendline), and a clear positive for gold (and by extension Bitcoin).

Lastly, we now have a market where almost all assets are moving higher.

When risky and safe haven assets rise simultaneously, you know disruption is here.

Asset owners are the only winners in this market.

Bitcoin is ripping, but many people remain sidelined.

Why?

People have been pissed off for over a year now. They are out here blaming Saylor for selling Bitcoin or thinking that BIP-110 was some existential crisis.

After prolonged periods of negativity, people become so used to the pain they forget what it's like to feel good again.

We like to think we are super logical creatures, but inside all of us is an emotional little kid who is mad that the orange coin didn't do exactly what we wanted, on exactly the timeline we predicted.

Last time I posted this I had people showing up saying that they were immune to emotions.

No dumbass. 

You're just blind to them.

You can't remove emotionality from our lives, but we can get better at navigating it and seeing when we are influenced by the tides of the crowd.

People are so traumatized after the past year that they (despite things looking incredibly positive for Bitcoin) are still in that same negative mindset.

Something shifted last week.

But sometimes our mood-based monkey minds are slow to pick up on the realities of the new world.

I think it's high time to embrace optimism again.
